content: Even up to two months after discontinuing the antibiotic, you should contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following symptoms: watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in your stool, severe stomach cramps, or a fever that begins after starting or finishing the medication. Blood Disorders: Oxacillin can cause blood disorders, including eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, and bone marrow suppression. Stop using oxacillin and seek medical attention immediately if you experience symptoms such as fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, headache, or an abnormally fast or irregular heartbeat. Liver Damage: Oxacillin may cause liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, weakness, unusual tiredness, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stool, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or the whites of your eyes (jaundice). Precautions: Who Should Not Use Oxacillin? Individuals allergic to oxacillin or any of its ingredients should not use this medication. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the specific oxacillin product you are prescribed. Important Information Before Using Oxacillin: Oxacillin is typically administered by a healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. If you store oxacillin at home, do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep oxacillin out of the reach of children. What to Tell Your Healthcare Provider Before Using Oxacillin: Inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any prescription or over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This information will help determine if oxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, discuss any of the following: Allergies to penicillin, other medications, corn, or corn products Asthma Liver or kidney problems A history of antibiotic-associated diarrhea Drug Interactions: Oxacillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Inform your healthcare provider if you are using any of the following: Tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) Probenecid (commonly used for gout) This may not be a complete list of potential interactions. Always provide a full list of medications and supplements to your healthcare provider. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: It is not known whether oxacillin affects pregnancy or harms an unborn baby. Inform your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Your provider will advise whether you should use oxacillin during pregnancy. Oxacillin passes into breast milk, so let your provider know if you are breastfeeding or planning to breastfeed. Overdose: If you or someone else has used too much oxacillin, seek medical help immediately, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Missed Dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. It is important to complete the full prescribed course of oxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of future infections becoming resistant to oxacillin or similar medications. Food and Drink Interactions: There are no known interactions between oxacillin and food or drinks. However, it is unclear whether alcohol affects oxacillin. Heavy alcohol consumption can weaken your immune response, making it harder for your body to fight infections. Always consult your healthcare provider for guidance.
